idiom_name: @volatile var cache: Option[T] recomputed under synchronized
implementation_notes: Scala has no properties with backing fields and no invalidatable lazy: `lazy val` computes once and can never be reset, so the realization is a private var cache: Option[T] (None = dirty) behind a public def accessor, plus @volatile for cross-thread visibility and synchronized (or a java.util.concurrent primitive) around the recompute-and-publish step. The annotation is Scala's spelling of the JVM volatile bit, so the same double-checked discipline as in Java applies - the accessor checks the option, takes the monitor, re-checks and publishes, in that order. Option carries the dirty/clean state without a second field and distinguishes 'not computed' from any value, but it does not make the recomputation atomic: only the flag's visibility is handled. Where the source is genuinely immutable, prefer deriving the value once or passing it explicitly rather than caching mutably.
pitfalls: `lazy val` is one-shot and thread-safe by construction but cannot be invalidated (a val cannot be re-assigned), so using it for mutable source data pins the first computed value for the object's lifetime.
Without @volatile or synchronization another thread can see a stale Some(...) next to a newer x, or a None forever; plain vars have no visibility guarantees across threads.
Option is not a null guard: Some(null) is a legal value, so a cache whose domain includes null needs a sentinel or an explicit Boolean flag instead of None.
synchronized on `this` is a public monitor that external code can hold; lock on a private object or use a java.util.concurrent primitive to avoid deadlocks.
